title: Umayyad Caliphate
capsule: The Umayyad Caliphate emerged from the First Islamic Civil War when Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, defeated and succeeded Ali ibn Abi Talib in 661, establishing Damascus as the caliphal capital and transforming the Islamic polity from an elected imamate into a dynastic monarchy. Under Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705) and al-Walid I (r. 705–715) the caliphate reached its greatest extent, with armies conquering the Maghreb and Iberia in the west and Transoxiana and Sindh in the east, while Arabic was imposed as the sole administrative language and an Islamic coinage system replaced Byzantine and Sasanian currency. Fiscal grievances among non-Arab Muslims (mawali) and the persistence of Ali's partisans fueled the Abbasid Revolution; in 750 Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah's forces defeated the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II at the Battle of the Zab, and the dynasty was extinguished—with the exception of the Iberian emirate—closing the caliphate our dataset records to 756.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Umayyad administrative geography is attested through papyri (especially from Egypt), literary sources (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari), and coinage; provincial boundaries in the Maghreb, Khurasan, and Transoxiana were fluid frontier zones and are reconstructed with significant scholarly debate; territorial extents carry moderate-to-low precision at the margins.
